name: Argus Lens

detectability.signature: Paired and quadrupled star images rotating slowly as the lens sweeps its orbit

proximity: The starfield visibly doubles and slides as parallax changes
contact: Every contact resolves into overlapping phantoms of itself
Targeting solutions multiply and contradict one another
prolonged_exposure: Chronic vertigo and headaches among bridge crews
Cumulative sensor misalignment requiring yard-side recalibration

phenomena: Gravitational lensing of background stars into rings and crosses
Magnified images of events that occurred thousands of years ago
Light bending that migrates across the sky as the lens orbits its unseen companion
hazards: Phantom contacts luring pilots onto false collision courses
Chronic sensor misalignment degrading long-range accuracy
opportunities: Natural telescope magnifying the deep past for astronomers
Data valuable to scientific institutions studying ancient light
known_incidents: Two mining claims were filed, abandoned, and refiled over the same asteroid because each party kept seeing different rocks
The observatory ship Clear Sight was commissioned solely to ride the fourteen-month sweep in perpetuity
description: Argus Lens wears the sky like jewelry. A diffuse mass of dark material half an astronomical unit across bends passing starlight into arcs, crosses, and slow-turning rings, so that any given bearing offers two or three versions of the same constellation. There is no surface, no glow, no edge; there is only the sky behaving beautifully incorrectly.

The lens drifts along a patient fourteen-month orbit around an unseen companion, sweeping its magnifications across different patches of heaven like a searchlight made of geometry. Approach it and the doubling tightens; nearby objects bloom into overlapping ghosts of themselves. Pilots learn quickly that the third rock over may be this rock, seen the long way around.

Astronomers found the Lens while chasing a supernova that seemed to detonate twice. What began as an embarrassment became the sector's finest natural telescope, magnifying light that left its sources millennia ago. Entire careers now depend on which strip of ancient sky the sweep is currently crossing.

The observation platform Clear Sight rides the orbit in permanent residence, selling deep-field imagery to universities and navies alike. Phantom-image collisions keep local traffic polite and slow. For researchers the Lens is a gift; for everyone else it is a standing reminder to trust radar over eyes.
